extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent prosecutors, and USPTO petitioners/practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for election-of-species/restriction practice in U.S. patent prosecution, especially how Markush claims, provisional elections, and claims to multiple species are to be handled and reviewed on petition. Covers applicable statutes, regulations, and MPEP procedures used to evaluate whether an election requirement and restriction are proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction under 35 U.S.C. § 121
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more independent and distinct inventions are claimed in one application, the Director may require the application to be restricted to one of the inventions. If another invention is made the subject of a divisional application complying with §120, it is entitled to the benefit of the original filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory basis for restriction requirements; restriction permits division into separate applications and protects divisional filings from being used as references against each other. The provision also states the validity of a patent shall not be questioned for failure to require restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election of species under 37 C.F.R. § 1.146
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first action on an application containing a generic claim (genus) and claims to more than one patentably distinct species, the examiner may require the applicant in the reply to elect a species to which claims will be restricted if no genus claim is allowable; if the application contains claims to more than a reasonable number of species, the examiner may require restriction to not more than a reasonable number of species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides regulatory authority for provisional election requirements in the first office action and for limiting the number of species examined where there are too many species. Election may be conditioned on the non-allowability of a genus claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claim examination rules (MPEP § 803.02 III.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following election, the Markush claim will be examined fully with respect to the elected species and further to the extent necessary to determine patentability; where a claim reads on multiple species, only one species needs to be taught or suggested by the prior art for the claim to be anticipated or rendered obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Markush claim is not allowable, the provisional election is given effect and examination is limited to the Markush claim and claims to the elected species, with claims drawn to species patentably distinct from the elected species held withdrawn. If applicant amends the Markush claim to exclude species anticipated/obvious over prior art, the amended claim will be reexamined; finality and entry of amendments are governed by MPEP §§ 706.07(a), 714.13, and 37 CFR 1.116 rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual exclusivity test for species restriction (MPEP § 806.04(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two or more species are claimed, a requirement for restriction to a single species may be proper if the species are mutually exclusive. Claims to different species are mutually exclusive if one claim recites limitations disclosed for a first species but not a second, and the second recites limitations disclosed only for the second and not the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed another way: to require restriction between claims limited to species, the claims must not overlap in scope. Overlap means shared limitations or scope; absence of mutual exclusivity counsels against restriction for that reason alone, but other factors (e.g., patentable distinctness, burden) still matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious burden standard for examining multiple species
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may require election of species when examination of multiple patentably distinct species would impose a 'serious burden' on the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of serious burden include requiring a different field of search (different classes/subclasses or electronic resources or different search queries), or when prior art applicable to one species would not likely be applicable to another (requiring substantially different search and analysis). The examiner must provide sufficient reasoning support for a finding of serious burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable distinctness criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Species are patentably distinct if they are not obvious variants of each other; if the examiner determines species are not obvious variants, they are patentably distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of patentable distinctness is fact-based and can be contested by applicant; if species are held patentably distinct, claims directed to nonelected species may be withdrawn from consideration following election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional election procedure and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: An election of a single disclosed species (or a single grouping of patentably indistinct species) may be required as a provisional election conditioned on a generic claim being non-allowable; the election serves as the starting point for examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provisional election is implemented in the first action when appropriate; if the elected species is rejected (anticipated/obvious), the provisional election is given effect and examination is limited to claims reading on the elected species. Applicants may elect a species with traverse and argue lack of burden or improper restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior art on Markush/Group claims (anticipation/obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Markush claim lists alternatives, the presence of the prior art disclosing one alternative is sufficient to anticipate or render the entire Markush claim obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: Fresenius USA, Inc. v. Baxter Int'l, Inc. — 'the entire element is disclosed by the prior art if one alternative in the Markush group is in the prior art.' Thus only one species need be taught or suggested by prior art to defeat a Markush claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal and reexamination consequences for non-elected species
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims drawn to species patentably distinct from the elected species will be held withdrawn from further consideration when a Markush/provisional election is given effect; if applicant later amends to exclude species rendered obvious, the claim will be reexamined to the extent necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant overcomes the prior art rejection by amending to exclude the offending species, the amended Markush claim will be examined again; if applicant obtains allowance of a generic claim, applicant is entitled to consideration of claims to additional species that depend from or require all limitations of the allowable generic claim under 37 CFR 1.141.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properness of a Markush group is not alone dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere presence of a proper Markush group does not by itself require that all members be examined together; members are only required to be examined together if there would be no serious burden and they are not patentably distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants cannot rely solely on labeling a claim as Markush to avoid election—examiner may still require provisional election and limit examination consistent with MPEP; applicant may contest but must address serious burden and patentable distinctness findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and finality of 37 C.F.R. § 1.181 petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition under 37 C.F.R. § 1.181 requests supervisory review by the Director of decisions (here, a Technology Center Director) regarding matters such as restriction/election requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director's decision on such petitions is final for the petition (no further reconsideration will be entertained regarding the election of species requirement in this decision); judicial review may be available upon entry of a final agency action adverse to the petitioner in the underlying proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and legal background of Markush claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Markush' claim recites a list of alternatively useable members; the listing of specified alternatives is referred to as a Markush group or grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and case law references supporting this definition include In re Harnisch, Ex parte Markush (Comm'r Pat. 1924), and Abbott Labs v. Baxter Pharmaceutical Products, Inc. See MPEP § 2117 for further treatment.
